title: Counting the Omer (Leviticus 23:15–16)
hook: forty-nine days counted from Passover to Shavuot

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seder: a meal in order, built so children will ask. Your line was ask the questions. What did you ask, and what did you hear? The seder is only the first night. Day one hundred thirty-six.

Think of the last time you counted days toward something. A trip. A wedding. A due date. A release date. Most of us count down: ten days left, nine, eight. We cross off the calendar, and the days in between are just in the way. On the second night of Passover, Jews start a count too. But it goes the other way. One day. Two days. Three. Every night for seven weeks, out loud, with a blessing. Nobody crosses anything off. They add. And if you forget a day, people notice.
screen: `MOST OF US COUNT DOWN.` → `THIS COUNT GOES UP.` → `EVERY NIGHT FOR SEVEN WEEKS.`

segments.voice: It comes from the Torah: "And ye shall count unto you" from the day the first sheaf of barley was brought to the Temple, "seven weeks shall there be complete," and then the fiftieth day is a festival. That first sheaf was called the omer. An omer is a measure of grain, and it gives the whole period its name: the Omer, and the practice, counting the Omer. Passover falls at the barley harvest. Seven weeks later comes the wheat harvest and the holiday of Shavuot. So the count ties two harvests together. Over time, the rabbis also saw it tying two events together: leaving Egypt, and receiving the Torah at Sinai. Freedom from something, and freedom for something. The count is the road between them. The way it's done is precise. Each night after dark, you say a blessing and then the number: today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer. You say it, not just think it. You count up. There's a small rule people love: if you forget to count one night, you can count the next day, without the blessing. But if you miss a whole day, many authorities say you keep counting every night, just without the blessing, because the chain was broken. The weeks have a sadder side too. Tradition remembers that many of Rabbi Akiva's students died in this season, so many communities keep some signs of mourning, like no weddings, until the thirty-third day, called Lag BaOmer, which is a day of bonfires and joy. The kabbalists gave each of the forty-nine days its own quality to work on. Counting up means each day is worth something by itself.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS SHALL THERE BE COMPLETE.` · `OMER: A SHEAF OF BARLEY.` · `FROM EGYPT TO SINAI.` · `SAY THE NUMBER OUT LOUD.` · then, large: `EACH DAY COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count one day tonight. Before that, settle, and breathe. Count your breaths up, slowly: one, two, three, up to seven, and start again. Don't rush to the end; there isn't one. Notice that each breath is complete in itself. Then think about something you're working toward. Instead of counting down to it, what would it look like to count up, one day added at a time? The bell holds the time.
Omer. A sheaf of barley, and the forty-nine days counted aloud, night by night, from Passover to Shavuot.
Your line: count the days up. Tonight, say out loud what day you're on in something you've started: a habit, a recovery, a new job. Day one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: From the second night of Passover, many Jews count the Omer each night after dark: a blessing, then the day and week (today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer), for forty-nine nights until Shavuot.

original.note: Hebrew: a sheaf, a measure of grain; the barley offering brought on Passover.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious countdown to a holiday.
what it means: forty-nine days counted up, aloud, tying freedom from Egypt to the gift at Sinai.

what a scholar hears: Leviticus 23:15–16; the Pharisees and Sadducees disputed when the count begins ('the morrow after the day of rest'); the mourning period recalls Rabbi Akiva's students (Yevamot 62b).

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Leviticus 23:15 ('And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest... seven weeks shall there be complete').
Forgotten night / forgotten day rules: Shulchan Aruch OC 489:7–8. Confirm.
Mourning customs until Lag BaOmer vary widely (some to day 33, some to day 34, some other periods). Phrased as 'many communities'.
Kabbalistic sefirot for each day mentioned briefly without detail.
Pharisee/Sadducee dispute over 'the morrow after the day of rest' (Menachot 65a); in trapdoor only.
